# Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs

Azim Ospanov ^(†)^(†)thanks: First author: azimospanov@outlook.com
Affiliation: Huawei Foundation Model Department Affiliation: The Chinese
University of Hong Kong    Zijin Feng ^(†)^(†)thanks: Corresponding
authors: fengzijinn@gmail.com, farnia@cse.cuhk.edu.hk
Affiliation: Huawei Foundation Model Department    Ding Ding
Affiliation: Huawei Foundation Model Department Affiliation: The Hong
Kong University of Science and Technology    Chengwu Liu
Affiliation: Huawei Foundation Model Department    Haoli Bai
Affiliation: Huawei Foundation Model Department    Jiacheng Sun

###### Abstract

Large Language Models (LLMs) have made remarkable progress on solving
competition-level mathematics, yet their ability to verify
natural-language mathematical proofs remains relatively underexplored.
This gap is especially pronounced for Olympiad-level proofs, which
require meticulous assessment of each claim in a long reasoning chain.
Current proof verification thus primarily relies on expert inspection,
which is costly to scale. In this paper, we present a systematic study
of LLM-based verification in this setting. Specifically, we introduce a
human-curated dataset of USAMO 2025 candidate solutions with expert
grading, and conduct a broad evaluation of existing LLM verifiers across
frontier models. We also propose TROJAN, an iterative self-critique
pipeline for generating high-fidelity adversarial proofs at scale. Our
comprehensive evaluation covers 20 models spanning seven metrics, two
prompt styles, three inference methods, and three prompt templates,
showing that state-of-the-art models still leave considerable room for
improvement. To narrow this gap, we propose MABGrader, a Multi-Armed
Bandit framework that reframes grading as arm selection over the
discrete score space. MABGrader outperforms the SOTA ProofGrader by
26.4% in Quadratic Weighted Kappa and reduces grading error by 14%. Code
and dataset are available at
[https://github.com/aziksh-ospanov/TROJAN](https://github.com/aziksh-ospanov/TROJAN).

## 1 Introduction

Figure 1: Performance of models on Trojan-Bench(H) , comparing
Majority@16 with our MABGr. inference method across 4 metrics. Color and
marker size denotes the model and parameter scale, resp. The spread
indicates considerable room for improvement, while MABGr. show
consistent gains.

Mathematical problem-solving is a core capability of large language
models (LLMs). Recent frontier models have demonstrated remarkable
proficiency in competition-level mathematics, including the
International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO) and the United States of
America Mathematical Olympiad (USAMO) \[[58](#bib.bib58),
[24](#bib.bib24)\]. Much of this progress, however, is measured by
final-answer correctness, which is a limited proxy for complex
mathematical reasoning since a solution may reach the correct answer
while containing logical gaps, unjustified claims, or subtle
errors \[[47](#bib.bib47), [33](#bib.bib33)\]. Moreover, many proving
problems do not admit a final answer, requiring costly expert
verification.

These motivate scalable methods for evaluating natural-language
mathematical solutions. In this work, we study the verification of
natural-language mathematical solutions. Specifically, an LLM-based
verifier receives a mathematical problem, a candidate solution, and
optionally a reference solution and a marking scheme; it must then
identify reasoning errors and assign a fair grade \[[33](#bib.bib33),
[4](#bib.bib4)\]. Recent work has approached this task by constructing
proof-verification benchmarks and designing LLM-based graders:
MathArena \[[4](#bib.bib4)\] evaluates LLMs on competition proof
problems using expert graders to assess model-generated solutions,
ProofAutoGrader \[[32](#bib.bib32)\] constructs IMO-GradingBench and
studies automatic grading with reference solutions and guidelines, and
ProofGrader \[[33](#bib.bib33)\] analyzes how model choice, grading
schemes, reference solutions, and ensembling affect agreement with
expert.

Despite this progress, two challenges remain for Olympiad-level
mathematical verification. First, existing datasets often collect
LLM-generated candidate solutions and rely on human experts to grade
them, which is costly, difficult to scale, and provides limited control
over the error distribution \[[4](#bib.bib4), [33](#bib.bib33)\]. This
makes it difficult to diagnose which types of mistakes LLM can or cannot
detect. Second, verification itself remains difficult. Competition
proofs are long, multi-step arguments in which a single mistake or
omission can invalidate later conclusions or alter the appropriate
partial credit. A verifier must thus go beyond surface plausibility by
localizing the failure point and assessing its effect on the final
grade.
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs")
illustrates this gap. Existing approaches, including prompt engineering,
PRM/ORM-based selection \[[29](#bib.bib29), [57](#bib.bib57)\], and
LLM-judge ensembles \[[8](#bib.bib8), [22](#bib.bib22)\], can improve
verification performance, but often require careful finetuning and
stacking of different models. These limitations motivate diagnostic
benchmarks for targeted error analysis and inference methods that
improve grading without modifying the underlying base model.

In this work, we present a systematic study of LLM-based verification
for Olympiad-level mathematics. We introduce a human-curated benchmark
dataset derived from the USAMO 2025, where rubric-aligned adversarial
errors, such as imprecise notation and unjustified lemma applications,
are deliberately injected into candidate solutions. This design enables
targeted evaluation of whether LLM judges can detect specific reasoning
flaws and assign appropriate partial credit, while providing greater
control over error type and severity than spontaneous LLM-generated
mistakes. To scale data generation, we propose an iterative
self-critique pipeline called TROJAN (Targeted adveRsarial errOr
inJection for mAth evaluatioN) that produces adversarial solutions with
human-like flaws. We show that fine-tuning on this synthetic data
improves agreement with expert grading. We further propose MABGrader, an
agentic Multi-Armed Bandit framework for mathematical verification.
Rather than producing a verification judgment in one pass, MABGrader
formulates verification as an optimal selection problem over candidate
judgments, where each arm corresponds to a possible grade with
supporting error analysis. Through iterative sampling and reward
optimization, it allocates more computation to uncertain cases and
improves grade selection without modifying the underlying base model.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:

- •
  We introduce Trojan-Bench(H), a human-curated dataset of
  error-injected USAMO 2025 solutions for evaluating how LLM verifiers
  detect subtle reasoning flaws and assign grades.
- •
  We propose TROJAN, a self-critique pipeline for generating
  high-fidelity adversarial samples, and show that training on the
  resulting Trojan-Bench(S) improves alignment with experts.
- •
  We conduct a systematic evaluation of 20 models across multiple
  prompts, inference methods, and metrics, measuring their verification
  abilities on Olympiad-level mathematics.
- •
  We introduce MABGrader, a Multi-Armed Bandit algorithm that mitigates
  LLM verification instability and provides a robust alternative to
  single- and multi-shot grading methods.

## 2 Related Works

#### Benchmarks for Mathematical Reasoning.

The mathematical evaluation includes foundational datasets such as GSM8K
\[[9](#bib.bib9)\] and MATH \[[29](#bib.bib29)\], alongside advanced
benchmarks like AIME \[[10](#bib.bib10)\], HARDMath2
\[[46](#bib.bib46)\], and CollegeMath \[[49](#bib.bib49)\]. Recent
research has focused on competition-level mathematics through
specialized benchmarks including Omni-MATH \[[18](#bib.bib18)\],
Olympiad-Bench \[[23](#bib.bib23)\], and HARP \[[63](#bib.bib63)\].
Modern frameworks such as MathArena \[[4](#bib.bib4)\] provide model
rankings based on challenging problems sampled from fresh Olympiads.
Beyond benchmarking, recent breakthroughs have led to systems that
participate directly in the International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO)
\[[24](#bib.bib24), [21](#bib.bib21), [53](#bib.bib53)\]. These
advancements demonstrate that models are moving toward achieving
performance comparable to top human competitors.

#### LLM-as-a-Judge in mathematics.

LLM-as-a-Judge frameworks utilize large language models to evaluate
responses based on metrics such as correctness and fairness
\[[22](#bib.bib22), [65](#bib.bib65), [28](#bib.bib28),
[52](#bib.bib52)\]. Recent studies on LLM reliability show that while
these models achieve high correlation with human experts on standard
tasks \[[48](#bib.bib48), [17](#bib.bib17)\], they remain susceptible to
issues such as sycophancy \[[43](#bib.bib43)\]. However, when grading
complex mathematical theorems, many researchers continue to rely on
human experts, a practice that limits the scalability of such evaluation
pipelines \[[33](#bib.bib33), [32](#bib.bib32), [59](#bib.bib59),
[42](#bib.bib42)\].

#### Verification in formal mathematics.

Complementing informal evaluation, formal mathematics utilizes proof
assistants such as Lean \[[34](#bib.bib34)\], Coq \[[5](#bib.bib5)\],
and Isabelle \[[35](#bib.bib35)\] to achieve automated verification.
Benchmarks in this domain rely on the underlying language kernel to
confirm proof validity, offering an objective alternative to natural
language assessment \[[64](#bib.bib64), [39](#bib.bib39),
[54](#bib.bib54), [62](#bib.bib62)\]. Recent research also employs
compiler feedback to guide LLM generation \[[38](#bib.bib38),
[30](#bib.bib30)\] and integrates informal reasoning steps into formal
proofs to enhance verifiability \[[40](#bib.bib40), [25](#bib.bib25),
[6](#bib.bib6)\].

#### Industry standards on fair grading.

According to \[[13](#bib.bib13)\], in math competitions with binary
grading, the agreement is approximately 90.4%. As we expand this to a
0–7 scale, the agreement and correlation will naturally be lower.
Although those figures are not directly translatable to our setting, the
consensus is that prestigious math Olympiads and new mathematical proofs
should have a high rate of agreement among judges and reviewers. The
intended gold standard involves multiple graders, a rubric, and a
reconciliation process, which is stricter than single-rater "good
enough" labeling. For general educational purposes, \[[60](#bib.bib60)\]
reports an absolute $`QWK_{human,LLM}\geq 0.70`$ as an acceptable metric
for automated scoring. This is not a universal rule of thumb, as
different domains have different requirements. We use these guidelines
as a conservative lower bound for model evaluation. In this work, we
systematically examine the current state of LLM grading to clarify the
performance of automated judging against human labels.

Figure 2: Example verification inputs for USAMO 2025 Problem 1 under the
Full and Blind settings. In the Full setting, the verifier receives the

In this work, we study the verification of natural-language mathematical
solutions. Given a mathematical problem $`p`$, a candidate solution
$`\tilde{s}`$, and optionally a reference solution Ref and a marking
scheme MS, the goal is for an LLM-based verifier to identify reasoning
errors and assign a grade that fairly reflects the correctness and
completeness of the solution. Following common practice in
 \[[4](#bib.bib4), [32](#bib.bib32), [33](#bib.bib33)\], grades range
from 0 to 7.

We consider two verification settings, illustrated in
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Problem Formulation ‣ Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs").
In the Full setting, corresponding to the Ref+MS configuration of
\[[33](#bib.bib33)\], the verifier is provided with both the reference
solution and the marking scheme specifying point allocations and
deductions. In the Blind setting, corresponding to the None
configuration of \[[33](#bib.bib33)\], the verifier receives only the
problem and candidate solution, without access to either a reference
solution or a marking scheme.

## 4 Dataset Construction

To comprehensively evaluate whether LLMs can verify Olympiad-level
proofs and assign appropriate grades, in this section we describe the
construction of our human-curated Trojan-Bench(H) benchmark and the
proposed data generation pipeline TROJAN, which we use to obtain dataset
Trojan-Bench(S) .

### 4.1 Human curated dataset

We construct Trojan-Bench(H) to support controlled evaluation of
LLM-based proof verification. Unlike existing datasets that collect
LLM-generated solutions and annotate them with human grades, we use a
backward construction procedure: starting from golden reference
solutions, we map proof components to marking-scheme criteria and
systematically inject errors that correspond to targeted point
deductions. We build our dataset Trojan-Bench(H) from the USAMO 2025
competition set, which contains six proof-based problems across multiple
areas of mathematics. Grades range from 0 to 7 according to the marking
schemes. We use the USAMO 2025 problems, reference solutions, and
marking schemes provided by MathArena \[[4](#bib.bib4)\].

Concretely, we construct candidate solutions by injecting subtle errors
into the golden solution, disrupting the proof structure and leading to
specific point deductions. For each problem, we randomly sample a target
grade and introduce errors designed to match the corresponding
marking-scheme deductions. Furthermore, when constructing faulty
solutions, we applied heavier penalties to fundamental parts of the
proof, such as operating in base-$`2n`$ in Problem 1 or establishing the
correct definition and structure of cupcake segments in Problem 6. A
logical gap in a fundamental step typically causes a cascade of point
losses across other criteria. The 2026 version of the USAMO in
\[[4](#bib.bib4)\] follows a similar logic by specifying overarching
deductions.

To account for the inherent variance in individual grading, we utilized
two independent annotators for the final dataset. We followed the data
creation pipeline from \[[45](#bib.bib45)\] to increase the validity and
reliability of the final set. However, we omitted the final step of
non-expert validation due to the specialized nature of mathematical
proofs. The result is a set of 48 human-verified USAMO 2025 candidate
solutions with a corresponding human grade and a justification. We
provide a detailed description of the creation pipeline and aggregated
metrics in the following sections, and a full datasheet can be found in
the Appendix
Section [A](#A1 "Appendix A Datasheets ‣ Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs").

Trojan-Bench(H)

#### Expert Inter-Rater Agreement.

Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.1 Human curated dataset ‣ 4 Dataset Construction ‣ Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs")
provides the agreement metrics for the human-curated dataset following
the procedure in \[[45](#bib.bib45)\]. The results show a Quadratic
Weighted Kappa (QWK) of 0.76 and a Pearson correlation of 0.89, which
exceed the performance of any of the evaluated LLMs and indicate strong
expert consensus. Scoring consistency is further reflected in the Within
Tolerance Agreement, where 85% of scores fall within 1 point
($`WTA_{\leq 1}`$) and 94% fall within 2 points ($`WTA_{\leq 2}`$).
Combined with a low systematic bias of $`\pm 0.08`$, these metrics
establish the human-curated set as a reliable gold standard for
assessing automated grading systems.

### 4.2 Synthetic dataset generation

To scale benchmark construction beyond manual error injection, we
introduce TROJAN, an LLM-based pipeline for generating adversarial
mathematical proofs. Given a mathematical problem, a reference golden
solution, a marking scheme, and a target score profile, TROJAN outputs a
proof whose errors are calibrated to be consistent with the specified
score profile, together with a structured grade justification.
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 Synthetic dataset generation ‣ 4 Dataset Construction ‣ Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs")
provides an overview of the pipeline.

The score profile specifies the target point allocation across
marking-scheme criteria. The generator LLM is given one human-authored
error-injection example for one-shot prompting and then analyzes the
marking scheme. For criteria assigned full marks, it is allowed to
closely paraphrase the corresponding part of the reference solution; for
each criterion with points losses, it is tasked with injecting errors
calibrated to the target score. The same LLM then performs self-critique
using a separate prompt. The goal is to isolate the parts that contain
mistakes and produce an explicit self-judgment. Its output is an
alignment judgment together with revision guidance. In the refinement
stage, the model applies the suggested revisions to the corresponding
proof blocks. This critique-refinement loop terminates once the
self-critique model accepts the current candidate
$`n_{\mathrm{alignment}}`$ consecutive rounds; if alignment is broken
before then, the streak is discarded and refinement continues with the
latest critique. The maximum number of critique-refinement rounds is
bounded by $`n_{\mathrm{iter}}`$.

The pipeline is general and can be applied to any problem set with valid
reference solutions and marking schemes. We construct a large synthetic
dataset Trojan-Bench(S) from four competitions: USAMO 2025, USAMO 2026,
IMO 2025, and IMC 2025, with problem statements, reference solutions,
with data sourced from the MathArena repository \[[4](#bib.bib4)\]. When
evaluating the synthetic data, we treat this grade and justification as
ground-truth labels. Experiments on the subset of Trojan-Bench(S) show
that it closely correlates with Trojan-Bench(H), suggesting good
alignment.

#### Audit of Trojan-Bench(S).

To further validate the quality of the proposed TROJAN, we performed a
manual audit of the Trojan-Bench(S) subset. We sampled 50 problems and
annotated using similar procedures as in the construction and audit of
Trojan-Bench(H). Each problem was verified by two experts and we present
the correlation, error and bias metrics between LLM and human assigned
grades in
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Synthetic dataset generation ‣ 4 Dataset Construction ‣ Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs").
We observe that generally the correlation is high and $`\sim 83\%`$ of
problems fall within one grading points. This generally indicates that
the proposed rubric-based error injection helps LLMs inject relevant and
appropriate synthetic errors into the correct solutions. We also report
the inter-annotation agreement in
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.2 Synthetic dataset generation ‣ 4 Dataset Construction ‣ Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs")
between the experts in this audit and show that the consensus was high
when grading, with all graded problems falling into $`WTA_{\leq 1}`$.
Combined, this shows robustness and overall high quality of
synthetically injected errors via TROJAN.

## 5 Our Approach

To address the difficulty of assigning fair grades to Olympiad-level
problems, we implemented a Multi-Armed Bandit (MAB) algorithm for grade
selection. Even with access to a mark scheme and a reference solution,
producing a grade outright is often hard. Prior work also suggests that
evaluating a pre-assigned grade together with its justification is
easier than scoring from scratch, since the candidate grade provides a
concrete anchor for assessment. \[[9](#bib.bib9), [29](#bib.bib29)\].
Independently, evidence from the LLM-as-a-judge and educational
assessment literatures shows that aggregating multiple independent
evaluators of the same candidate reduces individual-judge bias and
improves agreement with expert ratings ([55](#bib.bib55),
[65](#bib.bib65), [52](#bib.bib52), [16](#bib.bib16)).

Motivated by this, we first considered an A/B-style voting scheme that,
given a grade range, argues for one grade against another. This approach
is token-hungry: its token cost grows linearly with the number of
comparisons, and it wastes pulls on clearly sub-optimal arms whose
exploration cost is high. We therefore adopt UCB \[[27](#bib.bib27),
[3](#bib.bib3)\], a well-studied bandit algorithm which, to our
knowledge, has not previously been applied to mathematical grading. We
compare them in the Appendix
section [N](#A14 "Appendix N Effect of Multi-Armed Bandit algorithm on grading ‣ Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs").

At the core of our algorithm is a judgment-defense setup. For each
candidate grade $`g\in\{0,\dots,7\}`$, we prompt an LLM to justify the
grade and record its justification along with a self-reported
confidence. In the next phase, the same model, now prompted as a judging
oracle, selects arms and assigns rewards. This recovers the classic
stochastic bandit setting. After each round, MABGrader aggregates the
oracle’s rewards and updates the arm statistics, balancing exploration
and exploitation to converge on the grade closest to the underlying true
grade.

At round $`t`$, let $`N_{g}(t)`$ denote the number of times arm $`g`$
has been pulled prior to round $`t`$, let $`r_{s}\in[0,1]`$ denote the
reward observed at pull $`s`$, and let

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\hat{\mu}_{g}(t)\;=\;\frac{1}{N_{g}(t)}\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}r_{s}\,\mathds{1}\!\left[g_{s}=g\right],\qquad N_{g}(t)\;=\;\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}\mathds{1}\!\left[g_{s}=g\right]
``` |  |

denote the empirical mean and pull count of arm $`g`$. UCB first plays
each arm once, then at every subsequent round selects

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
g_{t}\;=\;\arg\max_{g\in\{0,\dots,7\}}\Big[\,\underbrace{\hat{\mu}_{g}(t)}_{\text{exploitation}}\;+\;\underbrace{c\sqrt{\tfrac{2\ln t}{N_{g}(t)}}}_{\text{exploration}}\,\Big],
``` |  |

breaking ties uniformly at random. The default $`c=1`$ recovers the
classical UCB1 bound of \[[3](#bib.bib3)\], which yields
$`\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{KT\ln T})`$ regret for $`K=8`$ arms with rewards in
$`[0,1]`$; the oracle’s 1-5 fairness Likert is rescaled to $`[0,1]`$ via
$`r=(\tilde{r}-1)/4`$. The parameter $`c`$ is user-controlled and can be
adapted to different problems. The design is compatible with any
single-arm sampling bandit, including Exp3, $`\epsilon`$-greedy, and
Thompson Sampling. For this study we chose a single, well-established
algorithm and leave a comparison with alternatives to future work. We
provide more details in the Appendix
Section [I](#A9 "Appendix I Hyperparameter 𝑐 ablation in MABGrader ‣ Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs").

## 6 Experiments

### 6.1 Experimental Setup

#### Inference Settings.

In all experiments, we fix the sampling parameters at $`top_{p}=0.95`$
and temperature $`t=0.1`$ to minimize LLM-induced variance during the
grading process. Unless otherwise noted, we employ the "thinking"
versions of the evaluated models. For models that support adjustable
reasoning effort, the setting was fixed to "high". Maximum token limits
vary by model and are detailed in the Appendix. The default testing
environment follows the MathArena template \[[4](#bib.bib4)\]. Every run
was initialized with a seed of 42. We explicitly indicate where an
alternative template was used for comparison.

All multi-sample experiments are performed at @16, where we sample 16
independent attempts from scratch. To evaluate Best-of-N methods, we
utilize two Outcome Reward Models (ORMs):
Skywork-Reward-Llama-3.1-8Bv0.2 \[[31](#bib.bib31)\] and
ArmoRM-Llama3-8Bv0.1 \[[56](#bib.bib56)\]. We also incorporate two
Process Reward Models (PRMs):
math-shepherd-mistral-7b-prm \[[57](#bib.bib57)\] and
RLHFlow/Llama3.1-8B-PRMDeepseek-Data \[[14](#bib.bib14)\]. For our main
MABGrader results we used 16 number of iterations and $`c=0.25`$ guided
by our ablation result.

#### Evaluation Metrics.

We use seven metrics to measure alignment between verifier-generated
grades and ground truth grades.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{QWK}`$ | $`\displaystyle=1-\frac{\sum_{i,j}w_{i,j}O_{i,j}}{\sum_{i,j}w_{i,j}E_{i,j}},`$ | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{WTA}_{\tau}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\{|y_{i}-\hat{y}_{i}|\leq\tau\},`$ | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{RMSE}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_{i}-\hat{y}_{i})^{2}},`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{MAE}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|y_{i}-\hat{y}_{i}|,`$ | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{Pearson}_{r}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{i}(y_{i}-\bar{y})(\hat{y}_{i}-\bar{\hat{y}})}{\sqrt{\sum_{i}(y_{i}-\bar{y})^{2}}\sqrt{\sum_{i}(\hat{y}_{i}-\bar{\hat{y}})^{2}}},`$ | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{EM}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\{y_{i}=\hat{y}_{i}\}.`$ |  |

Here, $`n`$ is the number of grading samples; $`y_{i}`$ and
$`\hat{y}_{i}`$ the ground-truth and verifier-generated grades for the
$`i`$-th sample, respectively; and $`\bar{y}`$ and $`\bar{\hat{y}}`$
their corresponding means. QWK measures ordinal agreement while
penalizing larger grade discrepancies, with $`O`$ and $`E`$ denoting the
observed and expected agreement matrices, respectively, and weights
$`w_{i,j}=(i-j)^{2}/(N-1)^{2}`$ over the $`N=8`$ possible grades. RMSE
measures overall grading error, WTA_(τ) measures the fraction of
predictions within tolerance $`\tau`$, Pearson $`r`$ measures linear
correlation, MAE measures average absolute grading error, and EM
measures exact grade agreement. We also report Bias, defined as
$`\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\hat{y}_{i}-y_{i})`$, with positive and
negative values indicating over- and under-grading, respectively.

#### Data Generation.

For synthetic data generation, we utilized Claude Opus 4.6
(Think) \[[1](#bib.bib1)\]. Because existing literature indicates a high
self-validation bias \[[7](#bib.bib7)\], we exclude this model from our
evaluation suite. We use a temperature of $`t=0.7`$ for data generation
and refinement, while the critic module employs a more conservative
$`t=0.3`$ to reduce variance in the feedback. We also finetuned two
models, Qwen3.5-9B and 27B SFT, on Trojan-Bench(S). The model cards are
specified in Appendix.

### 6.2 Analysis of Trojan-Bench(S)

#### LLM performance on the human-annotated benchmark.

We present the performance of 14 models on the human-annotated benchmark
using the QWK metric in
Figure [4](#S6.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ LLM performance on the human-annotated benchmark. ‣ 6.2 Analysis of Trojan-Bench(S) ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs").
In this section, we focus primarily on the correlation metric and
provide a detailed breakdown of all other metrics in the Appendix
Sections [D](#A4 "Appendix D Extended evaluation results ‣ Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs"),
[E](#A5 "Appendix E Extended Bar plots ‣ Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs")
and
[F](#A6 "Appendix F Evaluation of LLM correlation with human and other LLM annotators ‣ Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs").
Our evaluation spans two scenarios, Blind and Full, and incorporates
three sampling methods: CoT@1 (a single inference), MeanCoT@16 (the
averaged grade rounded to the nearest integer), and MajorityVote@16
(selecting the grade with the highest frequency).

Consistent with the findings in \[[33](#bib.bib33)\], the Full setting
is, on average, a less challenging task than the Blind setting. We
observe that models achieve a 0.06 higher absolute correlation and a
24.2% relative improvement in performance when using MajorityVote@16.
Interestingly, smaller models such as GPT-5-mini or Qwen3-8B achieve
higher correlation when not provided with additional information. Upon
further inspection, we found that these models are often unable to
follow the gold solution and instead produce hallucinated responses. A
deeper case analysis is provided in the Appendix
Section [J.1](#A10.SS1 "J.1 Behavior of smaller models on Full and Blind settings ‣ Appendix J Case studies ‣ Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs").
Overall, the models remain below the 0.70 threshold even when supplied
with full grading information and instructions, whereas expert
annotators achieve a 0.76 agreement rate. Furthermore, LLM performance
collapses to a maximum of 0.53 in the Blind setting. This scenario is
particularly difficult as the models must both derive a correct solution
and grade the attempt based on that derivation. We observe similar
trends in RMSE, Pearson correlation, and Bias, with the full suite of
results detailed in the Appendix
Sections [D](#A4 "Appendix D Extended evaluation results ‣ Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs"),
[E](#A5 "Appendix E Extended Bar plots ‣ Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs"),
and
[F](#A6 "Appendix F Evaluation of LLM correlation with human and other LLM annotators ‣ Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs").

![Refer to caption](2610.36767v1/bar_plot_qwk_main.png)

Figure 4: Model correlation with human labels using QWK across Full and
Blind settings. The bar plots report CoT@1, MeanCoT@16, and
MajorityVote@16 for each tested model.

Additionally, we conducted a comparative analysis of the different
sampling methods. Because we utilized a lower temperature, the
performance gap between single and multi-sampling is relatively small.
However, consistent trends remain present in our evaluation. On average,
MajorityVote outperforms other sampling techniques, though the primary
benefit serves to stabilize the grading output. Specifically, under Full
inference, MajorityVote scores 5.46% higher than CoT and 2.36% higher
than MeanCoT.

#### Quality of the Synthetic Dataset.

Furthermore, to evaluate the quality of the synthetic dataset, we
provide two points of analysis. First, we measured the QWK, RMSE, and
Bias on the USAMO 2025 subset of the synthetic data. We kept all
sampling parameters consistent across both sets, with each containing 48
samples. We present these results in
Figure [5](#S6.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ LLM performance on the human-annotated benchmark. ‣ 6.2 Analysis of Trojan-Bench(S) ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs").
Our evaluation suggests that on the human-curated benchmark, models
achieve a 0.07 lower absolute QWK, a 0.12 higher absolute RMSE, and a
0.04 higher absolute Bias compared to their synthetic counterparts.
These results indicate that the human-crafted dataset presents a higher
level of difficulty. While most models exhibit similar trends, we
observe that DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Thinking shows a significantly lower
correlation with synthetic data compared to the human-annotated version.
When measuring the correlation of model responses between the
expert-labeled and synthetic sets, we observe a Pearson $`r`$ of 0.89.

#### Fine-Tuning on Trojan-Bench(S).

Additionally, we performed SFT on the synthetic data and present our
findings in
Table [4](#S6.T4 "Table 4 ‣ LLM performance on the human-annotated benchmark. ‣ 6.2 Analysis of Trojan-Bench(S) ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs").
We supervised fine-tuned Qwen3.5-9B and 27B models \[[44](#bib.bib44)\]
using LLaMA-Factory \[[66](#bib.bib66)\] on the full set of our
synthetic data derived from four competition problems (see
Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Synthetic dataset generation ‣ 4 Dataset Construction ‣ Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs")).
The training mixture includes data from both the full and blind
verification settings. The data were split into training and validation
sets using a 95/5 ratio. The maximum context length was set to 16K
tokens, which is sufficient for our task. The 9B model was fully
fine-tuned, while the 27B model was fine-tuned with LoRA using rank-8
adapters. Both models were trained for 2 epochs with an effective global
batch size of 16, bfloat16 precision, and a cosine learning-rate
schedule with 10% warmup. The peak learning rate was 1e-5 for the full
fine-tuning run and 1e-4 for the LoRA run. All participating models were
run in "non-thinking" mode, which excludes the reasoning phase typically
enclosed in \<think\> tokens.

We observe that after fine-tuning, smaller models demonstrate improved
performance across the three primary metrics. Specifically, when trained
on synthetic data, models achieve a higher correlation with human
grading, a result that is consistent across both small and large model
scales. Taken together, these findings suggest that synthetic data
provides a high degree of correlation with human-generated labels and
that training on this data effectively improves agreement with expert
judgment.

#### TROJAN hyperparameter selection.

To choose parameters for our synthetic pipeline generation, we ablated
two main parameters. For each pair of parameters we asked human experts
to grade 10 outputs and aggregated LLM-assigned score (according to a
score profile) and human assigned scores. We report results in
Table [5](#S6.T5 "Table 5 ‣ LLM performance on the human-annotated benchmark. ‣ 6.2 Analysis of Trojan-Bench(S) ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs").
We selected $`n_{iter}=5`$ and $`n_{alig.}=2`$ for the TROJAN pipeline
as this configuration represents the global optimum across all primary
evaluation metrics. This setting achieves the highest correlation with
human labels (QWK = 0.884) and the lowest error (RMSE = 0.707). While
certain alternative configurations provide a zero bias, they do so at
the expense of significantly lower correlation and higher error rates.

### 6.3 Performance of MABGrader

#### Comparison with baselines.

Table [6](#S6.T6 "Table 6 ‣ TROJAN hyperparameter selection. ‣ 6.2 Analysis of Trojan-Bench(S) ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs")
presents the performance of four models from different providers across
the QWK, RMSE, and Bias metrics. To ensure a comprehensive evaluation,
we compare MABGrader against three primary baselines: zero-shot CoT@1,
MajorityVote@16 using three distinct prompt templates, and Best-of-N
selection utilizing four reward models applied to the MathArena template
outputs. Our results indicate that MABGrader consistently achieves the
highest correlation with human experts, as evidenced by higher QWK
scores across all tested models. While MABGrader significantly improves
RMSE and Bias for Kimi-K2.5, Gemini-3-Pro, and Qwen3.5-27B, we observe
that specific reward models such as RLHFlow and ArmoRM yield slightly
better results for DeepSeek-V4-Flash in terms of error magnitude and
systematic bias. Overall, the proposed method provides a more stable
alignment with human grading across diverse model architectures.

## 7 Limitations and Future Work

Our evaluation pipeline depends on the availability of both a markscheme
and a golden reference solution. This assumption is reasonable for
Olympiad-level grading, where they are produced alongside the
competition, but it does not hold for most real-world applications such
as peer review of new theorems or open-ended scientific verification.
Writing a high-quality markscheme without access to a reference solution
is itself a difficult task and remains an open problem that our work
does not address.

The same dependency limits MABGrader directly. Both the per-arm
justifications and the oracle reward are framed against the reference
proof, so the algorithm requires a markscheme that maps cleanly onto a
golden solution. MABGrader therefore does not apply to the Blind
setting, where there is no point of comparison for either the candidate
proof or the per-arm justifications. Extending the algorithm to
reference-free regimes, for instance by having the grader first
synthesize an outline of the expected proof that the oracle can then
evaluate against, is a natural direction for future work.

## 8 Conclusion

We conducted a systematic study of LLM-based verification for
Olympiad-level mathematics. We introduced a human-curated benchmark
derived from USAMO with markscheme-aligned injected errors and expert
grades, and used it to evaluate 20 frontier models across prompting and
inference settings. Our results show that current LLM verifiers still
fall short of expert-level agreement. We proposed TROJAN for scalable
adversarial proof generation to support evaluation and SFT and to
improve grading alignment. Finally, we introduced MABGrader, a
Multi-Armed Bandit method for verification that achieves the best
overall performance, outperforming ProofGrader with $`26.4\%`$ higher
QWK and $`14\%`$ less error. Our work suggests paths toward more
reliable automated verification.

Following the framework of \[[19](#bib.bib19)\] and

provides the additional information about our expert-annotated dataset
and
Table [8](#A1.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Appendix A Datasheets ‣ Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs")
provides additional information about our synthetically generated
dataset.

| Questions | Answers |
|----|----|
| Motivation |  |
|  For what purpose was the dataset created? |  The dataset was developed to benchmark the performance of current Large Language Models in grading and evaluating Olympiad-level mathematical proofs. |
|  Who created the dataset and on behalf of which entity? |  The authors of this paper. |
|  Who funded the creation of the dataset? |  The company where the authors work. |
|  Any other comment? |  None. |
| Composition |  |
|  What do the instances that comprise the dataset represent? |  USAMO 2025 problems that consist of problem statements, golden solutions, corresponding markschemes, candidate proofs with minor errors and corresponding expert assigned grades. |
|  How many instances are there in total? |  48 instances |
|  Does the dataset contain all possible instances or is it a sample of instances from a larger set? |  Yes, we present all instances. |
|  What data does each instance consist of? |  A problem statement, golden solution, corresponding markscheme, candidate solution with logical errors and corresponding expert grades. |
|  Is there a label or target associated with each instance? |  Only human assigned grades. |
|  Is any information missing from individual instances? |  No. |
|  Are relationships between individual instances made explicit? |  Not applicable. |
|  Are there recommended data splits? |  No recommended split. |
|  Are there any errors, sources of noise, or redundancies in the dataset? |  No, there are no errors in the proposed dataset to the best of our knowledge. Verification was done by two independent annotators. |
|  Is the dataset self-contained, or does it link to or otherwise rely on external resources? |  The dataset is self-contained. |
|  Does the dataset contain data that might be considered confidential? |  No. |
|  Does the dataset contain data that, if viewed directly, might be offensive, insulting, threatening, or might otherwise cause anxiety? |  No. |
| Collection Process |  |
|  How was the data associated with each instance acquired? |  All 48 instances originate from our team and further verified using two-step collection described in \[[45](#bib.bib45)\]. |
|  What mechanisms or procedures were used to collect the data? |  The seed problems were taken from USAMO 2025 subset of the MathArena repository \[[4](#bib.bib4)\]. Based on corresponding markschemes, we injected mistakes that would result in a particular loss of points. |
|  If the dataset is a sample from a larger set, what was the sampling strategy? |  No, there is no larger version. |
|  Who was involved in the data collection process and how were they compensated? |  Authors of this work are responsible for data collection. |
|  Over what time frame was the data collected? |  The dataset was collected over a four-month period, from January 2026 through April 2026. |
|  Were any ethical review processes conducted? |  No. |
| Preprocessing/cleaning/labeling |  |
|  Was any preprocessing/cleaning/labeling of the data done? |  Yes, we manually assigned grades to each sample and preprocessed the data to follow MathArena \[[4](#bib.bib4)\] format. |
|  Was the “raw” data saved in addition to the preprocessed/cleaned/labeled data? |  No, all raw data was converted to preprocessed samples. |
|  Is the software that was used to preprocess/clean/label the data available? |  We used open-source text editors to perform annotation. |
|  Any other comments? |  No. |
| Uses |  |
|  Has the dataset been used for any tasks already? |  We evaluated a large number of LLMs and measured their correlation with human labels. Moreover, we tested our proposed MABGrader agent. |

|  What (other) tasks could the dataset be used for? |  The dataset may be used for benchmarking alignment with human grades in LLM-as-a-Judge scenarios. |
|  Is there anything about the composition of the dataset or the way it was collected and preprocessed/cleaned/labeled that might impact future uses? |  We do not anticipate future issues emerging from the proposed benchmark dataset. |

|  Will older versions of the dataset continue to be supported/hosted/maintained? |  Yes. |
|  If others want to extend/augment/build on/contribute to the dataset, is there a mechanism for them to do so? |  Yes, since we release all accompanied information, others may use this data for other uses. |
|  Any other comments? |  No. |

## Appendix B Distribution of injected errors in Trojan-Bench(H)

Table [9](#A2.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Appendix B Distribution of injected errors in Trojan-Bench(H) ‣ Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs")
shows the distribution of injected errors in the Trojan-Bench(H)
dataset. During construction, we apply logical gap errors the most,
since they are easier to control and spot right away. Moreover, a
logical gap is the widest error category that is difficult to define
with one term, so many unjustified claims go under this broad umbrella
category. "Misapplied theorem" refers to errors with incorrect
preliminaries or even a completely wrong theorem used to prove the
statement. Conceptual errors refer to fundamental issues with the proof,
i.e., wrong constructions or even interpretations of the problem.
Computational slips are very minor mistakes that do not affect the grand
scheme of things, but still lead to less rigorous proofs. "Incomplete
justification" is a mistake in which the proof is only partially
complete and technically correct, but fails to explain all
conditions/steps.

## Appendix C Evaluated Model List

Table [10](#A3.T10 "Table 10 ‣ Appendix C Evaluated Model List ‣ Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs")
summarises every grader that participates in our evaluation suite. The
list spans 20 distinct models from major providers, covering both
open-weight and closed-weight families together with their
thinking-enabled and non-thinking variants where available. Each row
reports which (dataset, prompting style) combinations a given model was
run on. The two datasets are USAMO 2025 (the human-annotated benchmark,
Trojan-Bench(H)) and the synthetic set (Trojan-Bench(S)), and the two
styles are the rubric-equipped Full template and the rubric-free Blind
template. The final column lists the maximum completion-token budget
observed across attempts, which clarifies the inference-cost regime each
model operated in. We observe that models rarely hit the maximum token
limit.

In total, the table tracks 52 model$`\times`$(dataset, style)
configurations and serves as an index for the per-model results that
follow later in this appendix. Coverage is not uniform across providers.
Smaller open-weight reward-style models such as the Prometheus family
were evaluated on Trojan-Bench(H) Full only, since they did not produce
usable scores in the rubric-free regime. Frontier thinking-enabled
models were evaluated more broadly because their scoring behaviour is
the primary subject of our analysis.

Table 14: Mean $`\pm`$ standard deviation of RMSE, bias, and exact-match
accuracy across individual CoT sampling attempts per problem.
Thinking-enabled and non-thinking model variants are denoted by T and T,
respectively. Results are evaluated on the human-labelled
Trojan-Bench(H) dataset without access to a standard markscheme and
golden solution.

#### Correlation and error patterns on Trojan-Bench(H).

Across both Full and Blind templates, the strongest graders on
Trojan-Bench(H) are the thinking-enabled variants of frontier models.
Under the Full setting, DeepSeek-V4-Flash (Think) leads on most
aggregate metrics with mean Pearson $`r`$ of $`0.66`$, mean QWK of
$`0.63`$, and mean MAE of $`1.38`$ across attempts, closely followed by
GPT-5 ($`0.62`$ Pearson, $`0.56`$ QWK) and DeepSeek-V3.2 (Think)
($`0.62`$ Pearson, $`0.61`$ QWK). The non-thinking variants of the same
model families lose between $`0.05`$ and $`0.20`$ QWK and pick up
systematic over-grading bias, often exceeding $`+1.0`$ points. Smaller
open-weight graders such as Qwen3-8B, Prometheus-V2-7B, and
Prometheus-V2-8$`\times`$7B, together with GPT-4o, collapse to near-zero
or negative correlation with the human reference, with MAE close to or
exceeding $`3.0`$, which is the level of a constant "award full marks"
baseline.

#### Effect of aggregation.

Mean-CoT@16 and MajorityVote@16 produce small but consistent gains over
a single CoT call. Gemini-2.5-Flash improves from QWK $`0.59`$ at CoT@1
to $`0.68`$ at MeanCoT@16 in the Full setting, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash
(Think) improves from $`0.64`$ to $`0.69`$. MajorityVote@16 produces
similar gains except on graders whose all samples agree, in which case
voting cannot denoise a deterministic bias (a pattern we revisit in the
case-study section). The Blind setting shows the same ordering of
graders as Full but with a uniform downward shift in correlation, and a
sign flip in bias for several frontier models. DeepSeek-V3.2 (Think),
for example, moves from $`+0.27`$ Full to $`-0.88`$ Blind, which
reflects the absence of the rubric anchor.

#### Smaller graders behave differently on Trojan-Bench(H).

A non-trivial ranking shift appears for the small graders. Qwen3-8B,
GPT-5 Mini, and Kimi-K2.5 reach better QWK and lower MAE under the Blind
template than under the Full template. We discuss this counter-intuitive
effect in detail in
Section [J.1](#A10.SS1 "J.1 Behavior of smaller models on Full and Blind settings ‣ Appendix J Case studies ‣ Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs").
The short version is that the rubric in the Full template acts as a
surface-form anchor that biases small graders toward awarding most of
the available points on each rubric line.

### D.2 Trojan-Bench(S)

#### Correlation and error patterns on Trojan-Bench(S).

The synthetic benchmark is constructed so that every candidate solution
has a target rubric-aligned grade, which makes the Full setting easier
than on Trojan-Bench(H). Under the Full template, Claude-Sonnet-4.6
(Think) achieves Pearson $`r`$ of $`0.81`$ and QWK of $`0.75`$ at the
aggregated level; DeepSeek-V3.2 (Think) reaches $`0.81`$ Pearson and
$`0.77`$ QWK with MeanCoT@16; and GPT-5 reaches $`0.77`$ Pearson and
$`0.69`$ QWK. Both Mean-CoT and MajorityVote lift aggregate quality by a
few points relative to a single CoT call. MAE values cluster around or
below $`1.0`$ for the strongest graders, which means the synthetic
distribution is concentrated where rubric-following alone is enough to
recover the target grade.

#### Failure modes carry over from Trojan-Bench(H).

Two of the failure modes we observe on Trojan-Bench(H) also appear on
the synthetic data. First, GPT-4o has near-zero QWK ($`0.12`$) despite a
non-trivial Pearson correlation ($`0.53`$) and a bias of $`+3.37`$,
which is the signature of a grader that ranks proofs in roughly the
right order but inflates every grade to the maximum. Second, the
lower-tier graders (Kimi-K2.5, Qwen3.5-27B, GPT-5 Mini) carry a positive
bias of about $`+1.6`$ to $`+2.2`$, again driven by over-crediting
partially correct rubric items. Under the Blind template, the systematic
over-grading shrinks because the rubric anchor is removed, and most
graders move to a small positive or near-zero bias under
MajorityVote@16.

#### Cross-set consistency.

The relative ordering of graders is largely preserved between
Trojan-Bench(H) and Trojan-Bench(S). The top three graders on the Full
template are the same on both datasets, and the bottom three are also
the same. The absolute values are higher on the synthetic set because
the candidate distribution has lower per-rubric-item ambiguity by
construction, but the directional conclusions match. This cross-set
consistency is the basis for our claim in the main text that fine-tuning
on the synthetic set transfers usefully to the human set.

Each plot reports a single metric family (correlation, error, or
agreement) for one (dataset, style) pair, with three bars per model
corresponding to CoT@1, Mean-CoT@16, and MajorityVote@16. We include
them so that a reader can compare every grader and every aggregation
method at a glance for any single metric, without having to

The plots make the patterns from the previous section visually obvious.
Frontier thinking-enabled models cluster in the upper band of the
correlation plots and in the lower band of the error plots, whereas
smaller graders separate cleanly into a lower-correlation, higher-MAE
cluster. The agreement plots (Exact Match and WTA $`\leq 1`$) show that
close-but-not-exact agreement with the human reference is achievable for
most frontier models, while exact agreement remains low even for the
strongest graders. The synthetic-set plots show the same ordering as the
human-set plots but with a uniform upward shift in correlation and a
downward shift in error, consistent with the cross-set discussion above.

## Appendix F Evaluation of LLM correlation with human and other LLM annotators

The heatmaps in
Figures [18](#A6.F18 "Figure 18 ‣ Appendix F Evaluation of LLM correlation with human and other LLM annotators ‣ Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs")–[33](#A6.F33 "Figure 33 ‣ Appendix F Evaluation of LLM correlation with human and other LLM annotators ‣ Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs")
report pairwise agreement between every pair of graders in our suite
(LLM-vs-LLM cells) together with their agreement with the human
reference (LLM-vs-human row and column). Each figure covers one metric
and one dataset, with the upper half reporting the Blind template and
the lower half reporting the Full template. We include them so that the
inter-grader correlation structure is visible at a glance, since a
single number per (grader, metric) cell does not capture how strongly
graders agree with each other rather than with the reference. All
statistics cited in this section are recomputed from the MajorityVote@16
sampling that produced the heatmaps, and the discussion is restricted to
the 14 graders run on Trojan-Bench(H) in both templates, and the 8
graders run on Trojan-Bench(S).

The most striking pattern across both datasets is that hiding the
markscheme degrades ordinal agreement with the human reference far more
than it degrades the magnitude of grading error. On Trojan-Bench(H) the
mean Human-vs-LLM Pearson $`r`$ drops from $`0.50`$ to $`0.39`$
($`\Delta=-0.11`$), Kendall $`\tau`$ from $`0.42`$ to $`0.30`$, and QWK
from $`0.41`$ to $`0.33`$, yet mean absolute error is essentially
unchanged ($`1.99`$ vs $`2.00`$) and RMSE actually edges down slightly
($`2.71\to 2.60`$). The Trojan-Bench(S) set shows the same dissociation
more sharply: Pearson $`r`$ collapses by $`0.21`$ ($`0.67\to 0.46`$) and
Kendall $`\tau`$ by $`0.20`$, while MAE improves under Blind
($`1.83\to 1.74`$). Removing the markscheme does not cause judges to
pick wildly different absolute numbers, since they still place most
attempts within roughly one point of the reference, but it strips them
of the ability to order attempts correctly.

A second pattern is a near-universal sign flip in bias on
Trojan-Bench(H), and a much subtler one on Trojan-Bench(S). Under the
Full setting the average judge is stricter than the human (mean bias
$`=-1.48`$); under Blind that average flips to $`+0.51`$, a swing of
almost two grade points, and 10 of 14 Trojan-Bench(H) judges
individually change sign, including GPT-5 ($`-0.98\to+0.56`$), Claude
4.6 thinking ($`-1.23\to+0.13`$), DeepSeek v3.2 thinking
($`-0.10\to+1.08`$), and DeepSeek v3.2 no-thinking ($`-2.08\to+3.02`$).
Only Gemini 3 Pro doubles down on harshness without the rubric
($`-1.38\to-1.58`$), and GPT-4o together with Qwen3-8B remain stricter
than the human in both regimes. On Trojan-Bench(S), where the reference
is itself an LLM-rubric consensus rather than a human grade, only 1 of 8
judges flips bias sign, which confirms that the flip on Trojan-Bench(H)
is a real markscheme-versus-human-style effect rather than an artifact
of model calibration. Read together with the previous observation, the
markscheme behaves like a penalty list: when it is taken away, judges
default to a more generous approach.

The LLM-vs-LLM blocks of the heatmaps reveal that consensus between
judges itself depends heavily on the rubric and depends on it more
strongly than human alignment does. Under Full, the frontier reasoning
graders form a tight high-agreement block, with pairwise Pearson
typically above $`0.7`$ and pairwise QWK above $`0.6`$, well above their
mean agreement with the human reference. Hiding the rubric pulls this
block apart: on Trojan-Bench(H) the mean inter-LLM Pearson $`r`$ drops
from $`0.64`$ to $`0.44`$ and its pairwise standard deviation almost
doubles ($`0.15\to 0.28`$), with DeepSeek v3.2 no-thinking becoming
essentially decorrelated from every other judge ($`|r|\leq 0.30`$,
including $`r=-0.45`$ against GPT-4o) and GPT-4o losing all coherence
with the strong-reasoning cluster. The Trojan-Bench(S) inter-LLM block
weakens less under rubric removal (mean $`r`$ from $`0.63`$ to $`0.54`$,
$`\Delta=0.09`$), and there the gap between LLM-consensus and
Human-agreement actually flips sign: with the rubric, LLMs match the
synthetic ground truth slightly better than they match each other (gap
$`-0.04`$), but without it they revert to agreeing with each other more
than with the reference (gap $`+0.09`$). Per-model rubric gains are also
heterogeneous: frontier reasoning models gain large boosts (DeepSeek
v3.2 no-thinking $`+0.35`$ in $`r`$, Gemini 2.5 Flash $`+0.29`$, GPT-5
$`+0.18`$), whereas Qwen3-8B, Qwen3.5-27B, and Kimi-K2.5 actually lose a
small amount of human alignment when given the rubric. Taken together,
the markscheme is not a uniform injection of correct information but a
structural scaffold whose benefit scales with the judge’s reasoning
capacity, and whose absence pushes weaker judges toward random consensus
and stronger judges toward systematic leniency. The negative-rubric-gain
pattern for small graders is examined further in
Section [J.1](#A10.SS1 "J.1 Behavior of smaller models on Full and Blind settings ‣ Appendix J Case studies ‣ Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs").

## Appendix G Annotation procedure

Figure [34](#A7.F34 "Figure 34 ‣ Appendix G Annotation procedure ‣ Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs")
shows the custom web-based annotation tool that two domain experts used
to grade the 48 candidate solutions of the Trojan-Bench(H) benchmark.
The left panel lists the 48 problems with a counter at the top tracking
annotation progress. The main panel shows, in order, the problem
statement, the official marking scheme broken into criteria and their
point values, the golden reference solution, and the candidate solution
to grade. The annotator selects an integer score in $`[0,7]`$ from a
drop-down, writes a free-form justification, and advances to the next
problem. The tool stores annotations as JSON, which is the format we
used to compute the inter-annotator agreement reported in the main text.

We followed the two-pass procedure of \[[45](#bib.bib45)\]. Each
annotator graded all 48 problems independently. The disagreements were
inspected jointly, and a single consensus grade was committed for each
problem. The expert-vs-expert agreement statistics are reported in the
main text and indicate that the human reference is reliable enough to
serve as the gold standard for the LLM evaluation that follows.

![Refer to caption](2610.36767v1/figures/screenshot_grader.png)

Figure 34: Annotation website used by two domain experts to grade USAMO
2025 candidate solutions. The interface presents the problem statement,
marking scheme, golden solution, and candidate solution side by side,
and stores per-problem scores together with free-form justifications as
JSON.

## Appendix I Hyperparameter $`c`$ ablation in MABGrader

when the base grader is DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Thinking. We sweep
$`c\in\{0.10,0.25,0.50,0.75,1.00\}`$ and report QWK, RMSE, and bias on
the human-annotated USAMO 2025 benchmark with $`16`$ oracle pulls per
problem. The metric profile is non-monotone in $`c`$. Setting $`c=0.25`$
achieves the best QWK ($`0.657`$), the lowest RMSE ($`2.06`$), and a
near-best bias ($`-1.04`$). Larger values ($`c\geq 0.5`$) over-explore

plausible. We therefore use $`c=0.25`$ for all main-text MABGrader
results, paired with $`16`$ iterations as documented in

## Appendix J Case studies

### J.1 Behavior of smaller models on Full and Blind settings

A counter-intuitive effect emerges from our Trojan-Bench(H) evaluation,
where the three smaller LLMs we study, i.e., Qwen3-8B, GPT-5 Mini, and
Kimi-K2.5, correlate *better* with the human reference under the Blind
template (no rubric provided) than under the Full template (problem
$`+`$ golden solution $`+`$ markscheme). The Blind template strictly
removes information from the prompt, so intuitively, the Full template
should grade more reliably. Yet on Trojan-Bench(H) every one of the
three small graders has lower MAE and higher QWK under Blind than under
Full:

|            |               |       |                  |       |       |       |       |      |
|------------|---------------|-------|------------------|-------|-------|-------|-------|------|
| Grader     | Pearson $`r`$ |       | Kendall $`\tau`$ |       | QWK   |       | MAE   |      |
|            | Blind         | Full  | Blind            | Full  | Blind | Full  | Blind | Full |
| Qwen3-8B   | 0.196         | 0.180 | 0.154            | 0.186 | 0.175 | 0.076 | 2.44  | 3.07 |
| GPT-5 Mini | 0.458         | 0.519 | 0.337            | 0.436 | 0.455 | 0.421 | 1.77  | 1.92 |
| Kimi-K2.5  | 0.434         | 0.412 | 0.319            | 0.328 | 0.372 | 0.282 | 1.88  | 2.23 |

The QWK and MAE gaps are large (for example, $`+0.13`$ QWK and $`-0.36`$
MAE for Kimi-K2.5). Pearson $`r`$ and Kendall $`\tau`$ are also higher
with an exception of GPT-5 Mini. QWK and MAE penalise the much larger
errors the Full template commits on weak (0 to 2 points) answers.

#### Six concrete cases (two per model).

The six text boxes below summarise, for a single *(problem,
candidate-solution)* pair at a time, the verdicts the *same* grader
returns under the Blind and Full templates. Each box reports the mean
grade and the per-instance MAE under each template, gives an aggregated
per-instance gap, and excerpts representative free-form text from the
grader on each side. The cases were selected as the largest
Blind-vs-Full instance gaps within each model on the Trojan-Bench(H)
dataset.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### Global vs. local scoring.

The Blind template asks the model to "read the proof; output one number
$`0`$–$`7`$", which forces an *integrating* operation. A fatal flaw in
step 2 must reduce the credit step 5 contributes. The Full template asks
"for each rubric item, decide if the student earned the points", which
factors the task into *independent* per-line judgements. Small graders
are good at local pattern matching, for instance "does the student use
the words *Hall’s theorem*? yes $`\to`$ award the Hall’s theorem point"
(Cases C and E). They are weak at compositional reasoning, namely
"step 5 uses the bipartite graph from step 1; step 1 was wrong;
therefore step 5 is also wrong". The Full template omits the
compositional task by design, exposing the small grader’s weakness.
Larger LLMs such as Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, and DeepSeek-v4-Flash
propagate the error across rubric items since they consider local and
global grading patterns together.

#### The rubric is a high-precision surface-form matcher.

Every rubric line is, by construction, a description of the *correct*
proof’s structure: "Defining a graph", "Hall’s theorem", "Reducing the
problem", "Connectivity of construction", "Showing the graph is planar",
and so on. A student who reaches for the right tools but applies them
incorrectly produces text that contains exactly those keywords, so the
surface-form match is near-perfect even when the substance is wrong. In
Cases A, C and E the wrong proofs all *look like* the right proof. They
reach for the right theorem (Hall, induction, planarity) and follow the
right outline. Since the smaller models are less capable in uncovering
the smaller failures in each claim, they inflate the final score. In
Blind setting, there is no markscheme to base the reasoning on, so it
forces to inspect proofs closer, which inadvertently improves the
performance compared to the Full setting.

#### Reasoning revolves too much around the rubric and not the substance.

When the prompt says "this rubric line is worth $`3`$ points; explain
whether the student earned them", the small instruction-tuned model is
biased toward awarding most of the $`3`$. The default behaviour of small
instruct-tuned models is to follow the prompt’s expectation. The prompt
asks the model to "explain how many of the $`3`$ points the student
got", so the model produces a small downward adjustment from the maximum
(gives $`2`$ instead of $`3`$) rather than zeroing out. The Blind prompt
has no such anchor. The model has to commit to a number from
$`\{0,\ldots,7\}`$ after reading the proof, and the natural anchor
becomes the proof’s actual quality. This is why the Blind grader can
output a low value confidently when it sees a wrong proof, whereas the
Full grader output for the same proof rarely falls into the lower grades
territory, such as in Cases A, C, and E.

In summary, for a frontier grader, the rubric is additional context that
informs but does not override compositional judgement. For a small
grader, the rubric forces the model’s attention to it, and the LLM
behaves more like pattern matching and less like a proof verifier. This
effect is not present in larger models, since they verify the proof and
match the reasoning together with a markscheme that provides additional
context to how to properly distribute the grade. Strong vs. weak
compositional ability is exactly what separates the two evaluation
scenarios.

### J.2 Effect of MABGrader on grading procedures

We now study how MABGrader corrects the failure modes of vanilla
chain-of-thought (CoT) grading on the same proofs. Both methods use the
Gemini-3-Pro-Think model, the same problems and student solutions from
Trojan-Bench(H), and the same Full-style prompt (problem, marking
scheme, sample solution). The only difference is the inference
procedure: vanilla CoT corresponds to a single grading call (with $`16`$
attempts for the MajorityVote), whereas MABGrader runs the UCB procedure
with $`c=0.25`$, $`8`$ arms (one per candidate grade in
$`\{0,\ldots,7\}`$), and $`16`$ oracle pulls. The comparison is over the
$`48`$ datapoints.

#### Aggregate metrics.

MABGrader improves every aggregate metric. The biggest shift is in Bias:
CoT is consistently optimistic (mean signed error $`+1.383`$ grade
points), whereas MABGrader is closest to zero (mean signed error
$`+0.340`$). The QWK lift of $`+0.171`$ is the largest improvement we
observe from any prompt-engineering or aggregation (MajorityVote,
Best-of-N) methods in this paper.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Method | EM | MAE | RMSE | Bias | Pearson $`r`$ | QWK |
| Vanilla CoT (single attempt) | $`0.362`$ | $`1.660`$ | $`2.502`$ | $`+1.352`$ | $`0.511`$ | $`0.449`$ |
| Vanilla CoT ($`16`$-shot majority vote) | $`0.340`$ | $`1.681`$ | $`2.497`$ | $`+1.383`$ | $`0.515`$ | $`0.454`$ |
| MABGrader  (UCB, $`c=0.25`$) | $`\mathbf{0.447}`$ | $`\mathbf{1.277}`$ | $`\mathbf{1.957}`$ | $`\mathbf{+0.340}`$ | $`\mathbf{0.633}`$ | $`\mathbf{0.625}`$ |

Two observations follow. First, the $`16`$-shot MajorityVote variant is
no better (and slightly worse on EM) than the single-attempt baseline.
The 16 CoT samples agree with each other on $`38`$ of $`48`$ datapoints,
so voting cannot denoise a structural bias. Second, the gain in
instance-level MAE is asymmetric across the human-grade range. Vanilla
CoT is monotonically lenient on the lower band of the scale (mean signed
error $`+2.60`$ at human grade $`0`$, $`+2.67`$ at human grade $`2`$)
and slightly lenient on the upper band, with perfect proofs graded
correctly. MABGrader better matches grades on the lower end (mean signed
error drops to $`+0.40`$ at human grade $`0`$ and to $`+1.00`$ at human
grade $`2`$), while introducing a small under-grading of about $`-1`$
point at human grades $`4`$, $`5`$, and $`6`$.

#### Two concrete cases.

The two text boxes below illustrate the two failure modes vanilla CoT
exhibits on this benchmark. Each box reports the predicted grade and the
per-instance MAE for both methods, and excerpts representative free-form
text from the model in each role. The grading CoT was compressed for
better readability.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### Hypothesis enumeration via arms.

Vanilla CoT is a free generation: the model decides on the spot what the
grade should be, writing a chain of thought that can drift toward a
conclusion which is then rationalised against the rubric. The
arm-generation phase of MABGrader does the opposite. It runs $`8`$
separate calls, each of which assumes the answer is grade $`k`$ and
produces the strongest possible defence of grade $`k`$. Low-grade
defences end up surprisingly compelling because they do not have to wave
away foundational errors (Case G). The model is now arguing against its
own default rather than rationalising it.

#### Oracle as adversarial verifier.

The oracle is a separate model call that scores each arm’s defence on a
Likert scale, mapped to a $`[0,1]`$ reward. The oracle does not have to
commit to a number; it just has to ask whether each defence holds up
against the source. That framing is much easier for the model than
open-ended grading. In Case H the oracle returns full reward for both
the lenient and the strict reading of the off-by-one, since both are
individually plausible.

#### UCB tie-breaking is a strict-grading prior.

When several arms tie at maximum reward, UCB returns the arm with the
lowest id. Because arm ids equal candidate grades, "lowest id" means
"lowest grade". When the evidence is ambiguous between "give credit" and
"do not give credit", a professional grader defaults to the latter (the
proof should remove ambiguity). In Case H this tie-breaker alone is what
recovers the correct human grade.

#### Why self-consistency cannot close the gap.

A natural counterpoint is that the gain might be variance reduction and
that a simpler "sample CoT more times and apply MajorityVote" strategy
would close it. The aggregate table refutes this: the $`16`$-shot
MajorityVote variant is slightly worse than a single sample, and the 16
samples agree with each other on the large majority of cells.
Token-level sampling on a deterministic prompt with strong prompt-side
bias does not produce diverse enough gradings to escape the bias. The
diversity in MABGrader comes from the prompt side (eight different
"assume answer $`=k`$" prompts), not from token-level sampling.

In summary, the dominant LLM grading failure on this benchmark is
over-grading bias, not stochastic noise. Variance-reduction methods
(sampling and voting) do not address bias because the bias is
deterministic.

## Appendix M Benchmarking TROJAN SFT pipeline against ProofBench

Table [37](#A13.T37 "Table 37 ‣ Appendix M Benchmarking TROJAN SFT pipeline against ProofBench ‣ Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs")
presents additional evaluation results on
ProofBench \[[33](#bib.bib33)\], a dataset of LLM-generated proofs for
competition-level mathematics paired with expert human grade
annotations. For this experiment, we fine-tuned two models (Qwen3.5-9B
and Qwen3.5-27B) on synthetic samples generated by our TROJAN pipeline,
mirroring the setup described in the main text. We strictly excluded any
overlap between the ProofBench dataset and our training set. This
ensures that performance improvements stem from genuine learned grading
capabilities rather than data contamination or overfitting. We report
results for both the Full setting (which provides access to the
markscheme and golden solution) and the Blind setting (which provides
neither).

We observe that despite being fine-tuned exclusively on synthetic data,
the models achieve correlation levels with ground-truth labels that
match or exceed baselines, alongside a general reduction in overall
error and bias. This consistent improvement demonstrates that our
proposed markscheme-aligned synthetic error injection is both a robust
evaluation proxy and an effective method for generating training data
that aligns with expert human judgment. While the distributions of
synthetic and naturally occurring errors inherently differ, our results
reveal a functional overlap. Because the fine-tuned base model shows
improved performance on an entirely independent problem set with a
different group of expert annotations, it is clear that TROJAN’s
synthetic errors generalize to real-world mistakes and unseen grading
tasks. Furthermore, our generation pipeline provides fine-grained
control over the exact type and location of injected mistakes, offering
a targeted approach to further refine LLM grading capabilities.
````
